summary: ICSME 2026 mining study of 4,882 agent-generated PRs (532 Java across 68 repos, 4,350 Python across 448 repos) from AIDev v3, produced by Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code and Devin. Half of code-changing PRs include no test changes; in the buildable subset (213 Java / 1,664 Python merged PRs) existing tests cover 61.5% of changed Java lines and 27.0% of Python lines; agent-written tests raise diff coverage on average but only in 35.9% (Java) / 22.5% (Python) of Code+Tests PRs; try/catch lines are missed 86.0% (Java) and 81.0% (Python).

claims.claim: Only 49.6% of PRs that change code under test include test changes
claims.evidence: §IV-A: 2,176 of 4,387 code-changing PRs include test changes; Fig. 1 Venn. Purely descriptive; no human-authored PR comparison, so it is unknown whether agents differ from developers.

claims.claim: Existing tests cover 61.5% of agent-changed lines in Java and 27.0% in Python; 64.8% of Python PRs have zero covered changed lines
claims.evidence: §IV-B RQ2a: file-level aggregate over 259 Java files and 2,696 Python files; 1079/1664 Python PRs zero coverage; Fig. 2. Java subset is only 10 buildable repos that are smaller than the population (29K vs 102K LOC median).

claims.claim: Agent-written tests significantly raise diff coverage (+15.6 pp Java, +9.6 pp Python) but only a minority of PRs gain
claims.evidence: Table I with one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank (p<0.001); 23/64 Java and 136/605 Python PRs improve. Java figure rests on 64 PRs.

claims.claim: Error-handling constructs are most under-tested (Try-Catch miss 86.0% Java, 81.0% Python)
claims.evidence: §IV-B construct analysis with srcML tags; table near line 430s. Also no human baseline, and error paths are commonly under-tested in human code too.

claims.claim: Agents need coverage-aware feedback loops before submitting PRs
claims.evidence: Recommendation in §V derived from the findings; not tested experimentally.

patterns.note: Passing existing tests is weak evidence: those tests often never execute the agent's changed lines, so test-pass verifier loops need diff-coverage checks.
Unprompted agents do not reliably write tests that exercise their own changes (gain in only 22.5-35.9% of Code+Tests PRs; Java non-improving PRs show 2.6x test deletions vs additions).
Field data from real GitHub repositories and merged PRs across five agents.
Argues SWE-bench-style pass-the-tests metrics ignore whether tests exercise agent-introduced code.
Recommends human review prioritize error-handling paths.

methodology.sample: 4,882 PRs for RQ1; RQ2 coverage on 213 Java PRs (10 repos) and 1,664 Python PRs (34 repos) that built and instrumented; paired with/without-tests analysis on 64 Java and 605 Python PRs
methodology.baselines: none against human-authored PRs; within-PR with vs without agent tests
methodology.models: five commercial agents (Codex dominant: 1,018 of 1,278 Java and 5,209 of 7,191 Python PRs before filtering); no per-agent breakdown reported
methodology.variance: Wilcoxon signed-rank significance; distributions shown; no CIs on headline percentages
methodology.ablations: by PR category and syntactic construct

standards.peer_review: to appear at ICSME 2026 (emerging-results style, 12 pages)
standards.artifacts: replication package and dataset of patches, coverage reports, labeled lines (github.com/SageSELab/Agentic-Pull-Request-Test-Coverage)

biases.detail: Coverage analysis only on merged PRs from repos that build and instrument; Java subset is 10 smaller-than-average repos.
AIDev PRs are dominated by Codex, so 'agents' largely means Codex; no per-agent results.
Without coverage numbers for comparable human PRs in the same repos, the paper cannot show agents are worse than developers.
Line diff coverage measures execution, not assertion strength; covered lines may be unchecked.

coi.affiliations: University of Central Florida; George Mason University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, Devin (third-party, evaluated critically)
coi.detail: Academic, publicly funded; no product promoted.

verdict_reason: Solid, reproducible, peer-reviewed mining study with Java data, but the coverage subset is small and survivor-biased, results are Codex-dominated, and there is no human-PR baseline to show agents are worse than developers.
applicability: Directly usable for a Java team: do not treat 'mvn test passes' as evidence that an agent's change was tested. Add a host-agnostic, deterministic diff-coverage gate (JaCoCo with a diff-coverage tool in CI) that applies to PRs from any agent host, and require tests for added lines, especially catch/throw blocks in ingestion parsers and delivery error paths, where Java miss rates were 86%. In spec-driven development, tie each acceptance criterion to a test that executes the changed lines; across >=4 ingestion repos, enforce the same gate in each repo's CI rather than trusting a cross-repo integration suite to cover them. Watch for agents deleting tests (2.6x deletion ratio in non-improving Java PRs).

conflicts_with.detail: That position paper argues agents can replace human code review; this paper's field data show agent PRs are often untested and passing suites rarely exercise agent changes, undercutting removal of human/quality gates.
